opus-5.5.text:
I think it's quite understandable, and in some ways it's a very rational choice.

In a large company, even a very good one, a young researcher is usually one piece of a huge machine. The direction is often set from above, compute is allocated through layers of planning, and when a big project succeeds, it's hard for any one person to say, "this part was mine." You may get stability, a good salary, and access to enormous resources, but your sense of ownership can be weak. For people who are ambitious and want to leave a mark, that's frustrating.

A smaller lab, what people now call a "neolab," offers something different. The team is small, so every person matters. You can propose an idea on Monday and try it by Wednesday. You talk directly with the founders, and you shape the research agenda rather than just executing it. There's also the equity: if the bet works, the upside is very large. For someone in their twenties with fewer family obligations, taking that risk makes sense.

There's also a deeper reason. Many people feel the current paradigm, scaling large models with more data and compute, is dominated by a few big players, and it's hard to compete on pure scale. So the interesting question becomes: is there a different path? New architectures, better reasoning, more efficient learning, a better understanding of *why* these models work. Small labs are often founded around a specific thesis like that, and young researchers who believe there's something beyond brute-force scaling are naturally attracted to them.

That said, I'd add a word of caution. Small companies carry real risks. Compute is expensive, funding can dry up, and if the founding thesis turns out to be wrong, the company may not survive. And in a small company you're also expected to do many things beyond research: engineering, infrastructure, sometimes even product. That's a great learning experience, but it's not for everyone.

So my view is: it depends on what you want. If you want to deeply understand something and push one idea all the way, a small, focused team can be wonderful. If you want breadth, mentorship, and a stable environment to grow, a large company still has a lot to offer. What matters most is that you're working on a problem you truly care about, because in this field things change so fast that the problem itself, not the company label, is what keeps you going.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually a very natural and healthy thing, and I'd interpret it on a few levels.

First, there's the question of what you actually get to do. At a large company, the infrastructure is incredible, the compute is there, the data is there, but the frontier model effort tends to be concentrated in a relatively small group. If you're a young researcher joining, you may end up owning one piece of a very large pipeline. You learn a lot about scale, but your personal contribution can feel diluted. At a small company like NeoLabs, the team is maybe a few dozen people, and every person has to touch the whole stack. You see data, pretraining, post-training, evaluation, infrastructure, all of it. For someone early in their career, that breadth is enormously valuable. You develop taste much faster, because you're forced to make decisions that actually matter rather than optimizing within a fixed framework somebody else designed.

Second, there's the question of research freedom versus product pressure. Big labs today are also companies with products, and the roadmap is increasingly driven by what ships next quarter. A small lab, at least in its early phase, can afford to be a bit more opinionated. It can say, we believe this particular direction, whether that's a new architecture, a new way of doing reasoning, or a different approach to data, and we're going to bet the company on it. Young researchers are drawn to that clarity. They want to be in a place where the mission is one sentence long and everyone believes it.

Third, and I think this is underappreciated, there's a sense that the field is still open. Five years ago many people assumed the game was decided, that only two or three organizations could train frontier models. What we've seen since then, with smaller teams producing surprisingly strong models, is that the barrier is lower than people thought. Not zero, certainly, you still need serious compute and serious engineering, but good ideas and a tight team can still move the frontier. When young people see that, of course they want to try. That's the same instinct that built the big companies in the first place.

Now, I don't want to romanticize it. Small companies carry real risk. Compute access can be fragile, funding can dry up, and if the core bet is wrong, there's no second division to transfer into. And large companies offer things that are genuinely hard to get elsewhere: exposure to problems at a scale nobody else sees, mentorship from people who have done this many times, and the stability to do longer-horizon work.

So my honest advice to young researchers is usually this: don't choose based on size alone. Choose based on who you'll learn from and whether you'll be in the room where real decisions get made. If a small company gives you that, go. If a big company gives you that, also go. The worst outcome is not picking the wrong size. It's spending your most creative years somewhere you're not actually learning.

astra-6.text:
I think it reflects a desire to have more ownership over research. In a small company, a young researcher may be able to shape the direction, work on several parts of a problem, and see more directly how their contribution affects the outcome. That can be very attractive, even when the resources are more limited.

Large companies offer a different set of advantages: compute, infrastructure, experienced colleagues, and the ability to pursue projects at scale. But your role can also be narrower, and you may spend more time coordinating before you can test an idea.

So I wouldn’t interpret this simply as small companies becoming better than large companies. It’s a question of what kind of environment helps someone grow. For a young researcher, I think the important questions are: Who will I work with? Will I have room to develop my own judgment? And can I actually pursue the problems I care about?

sol-6.1.text:
I think young researchers are often choosing an environment where they feel they can make a difference. At a small company like NeoLabs, you may have more ownership over the research direction, work closely with the founders, and see your ideas turn into something concrete very quickly. That can be appealing, especially if you have a strong conviction about what to work on.

Large companies offer a different set of advantages: compute, infrastructure, experienced colleagues, and the ability to pursue projects at scale. But you may also spend more time coordinating across teams, and have less control over the overall direction.

So I wouldn’t interpret interest in small companies as simply a rejection of large companies. It reflects different priorities and different stages of a career. The important questions are: Who will you learn from? Will you have the resources to test your ideas? And will you actually be able to work on the problems you care about?
